sources.note: Section 'Suprasegmentals (tone, stress, length)' (p. 2) contains one sentence only: 'The final vowel in a verb may be greatly lengthened to indicate an unusually prolongation of the action.' No statement of where stress falls; the only other mention is 'Conventions: Phonological': '[j] occurs as an allophone of /i/ when unstressed and before a vowel.' Example words are unmarked for stress.

sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Comparative/historical only: 'Stress appears to have been contrastive (cf. /*ka'ɸuto/ "smoke" vs. /*gene'ɸo/ "bandicoot") but has not been reconstructed below.' Also 'One exception in Mubami is likely due to stress'. Hoyahoya forms cited from Carr (1991, 2006) carry stress marks in varying positions (117 of 333 cited forms marked: e.g. 'beno 'shoulder', 'koibo 'cassowary' vs ma'ha 'pig', ku'ti 'belly', ba'hai 'leaf'; 'geneho 'bandicoot' vs ke'muku 'knee', ki'oku 'heavy'). No synchronic stress rule stated for Hoyahoya.
